opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the simplest answer is that the economics of deployment haven't changed even as the frontier has moved. The biggest models are the ones that push capabilities forward, but they're rarely the ones you want to serve to millions of users. They're expensive and slow, and for most queries you don't need all that capacity. So there's always going to be a gap between the best model you can train and the model you can actually afford to run at scale, and distillation is one of the most effective ways we have to close it.

There's a deeper reason too. When you train a small model directly on raw data, you only give it the hard label, the one next token that actually appeared. A teacher model gives you a whole distribution over what could have come next, so you also learn which alternatives were plausible, which were nearly right, and how uncertain the teacher was. That's a much richer signal per example. As teachers get better, that signal gets better, so larger models make distillation more valuable, not less.

A lot of my work has looked at doing this on-policy. The classic setup is the student imitating teacher-generated text, but then at inference the student makes its own mistakes and ends up in states it never saw during training. If you let the student generate and have the teacher give feedback on the student's own outputs, you get much better results. It's similar to the difference between watching someone play chess and having a coach correct your moves as you play.

Finally, distillation is quietly behind a lot of the progress people credit to other things. Synthetic data, reasoning traces from strong models, self-improvement loops all have a distillation component: some stronger process makes better outputs and you compress that back into a model. So I don't see it going away. If anything, as we spend more compute at inference time on things like long chains of reasoning, distilling that behavior back into cheaper, faster models will matter even more.

r001.rationale: The response says the largest models are expensive and slow to serve at scale, so deployment requires balancing capability against what can be afforded.

r002.rationale: The response discusses serving models at scale but does not identify fitting very large models on smartphones as a motivation.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest framing is that distillation is a way of converting compute you've already spent into compute you can afford to spend at inference time. Training a frontier model is enormously expensive, and most of what that model learns is sort of latent in its outputs. Distillation lets you extract that knowledge into something smaller that's actually deployable at scale.

And the reason it doesn't go away as models get larger is that the gap between the biggest model you can train and the biggest model you can serve keeps widening. Inference costs scale with the number of parameters and the number of tokens, and if you're running something billions of times a day, you simply can't serve the frontier model to everyone. So there's always going to be demand for a smaller model that captures as much of the frontier model's capability as possible.

The more interesting point, I think, is that distillation is also just a better training signal than next-token prediction on raw data. When you train on the teacher's distribution instead of hard labels, you're getting much richer information per token. The teacher is telling you not just what the right answer is but how confident it is, what the plausible alternatives are. And on reasoning tasks in particular, sampling from the teacher and training on those traces gives you data that's better than most of what exists on the internet, because the internet mostly doesn't contain careful step-by-step reasoning.

One thing we found in our work on on-policy distillation is that it matters a lot where the training data comes from. If you only train the student on the teacher's samples, there's a distribution mismatch: at inference time the student generates its own tokens, makes its own mistakes, and it's never seen the teacher's feedback on those mistakes. So you sample from the student and have the teacher provide the signal on the student's own trajectories. That ends up being much more robust, and it's closer in spirit to RL than to supervised learning.

So I'd say distillation stays valuable because it sits at the intersection of two things that only become more important over time: the economics of serving models, and the quality of the training signal. Larger models make both of those pressures stronger, not weaker.

r001.rationale: The response explains that serving the frontier model broadly is too costly, creating demand for smaller models that retain as much capability as possible—a cost–performance tradeoff.

r002.rationale: The response discusses serving costs and deployability at scale, but does not identify inability to fit very large models on smartphones as a motivation.

astra-6.text:
I think distillation remains valuable because the model you can afford to train isn’t necessarily the model you can afford to serve. You might have a very capable large model, but for a particular application you care about latency, cost, and how often you can call it. Distillation is a way to transfer some of that capability into a smaller model that fits those constraints.

And as the larger models improve, they become better teachers. They can provide richer supervision than just a correct answer—they can generate examples and demonstrate how to approach a problem. The challenge is making sure the smaller model learns something that generalizes, rather than just imitating the teacher’s outputs. So scaling and distillation are complementary: scaling pushes the capability frontier, and distillation helps make those capabilities more practical to use.

r001.rationale: The response says a large model may be affordable to train but not serve, and that distillation transfers capability to a smaller model to meet latency and cost constraints.

r002.rationale: The response motivates smaller models with serving constraints generally, but does not mention smartphones or the difficulty of fitting very large models on them.

sol-6.1.text:
I think as models get larger, the gap between what we can train and what we can afford to deploy becomes more important. You might be willing to spend a lot of compute to build a really capable teacher, but you don’t necessarily want to pay that cost for every user request. Distillation gives you a way to transfer some of that capability into a smaller, faster model.

And the teacher can provide much richer supervision than a hard label. It can show how to approach a problem, generate useful examples, and expose distinctions that are difficult to capture in a conventional dataset. The student won’t recover everything the teacher knows, but for a particular task or deployment budget, it can be a very good tradeoff. So larger models actually make distillation more interesting: you have stronger teachers, and a stronger incentive to make their capabilities accessible.

r001.rationale: The response says a smaller, faster student can deliver some of a teacher’s capability at lower deployment cost, describing a task- and budget-specific tradeoff.
